selection_rule: top-k species by (n_distinct_proposers, n_members, stable sha256); representative = member with smallest sha256(pid)

selected.name: Mechanistic Explanatory Depth
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives a causal account of why the method addresses the stated failure and derives testable implications; score 0 when it merely introduces components and asserts usefulness.
selected.rationale: R06, R20, and R60 explicitly connect architectural behavior to signal propagation, latent concepts, or adversarial vulnerability, unlike abstracts with primarily procedural descriptions.
member_names: Experiments probe the stated explanation, not just the headline metric
Mechanistic explanation of a phenomenon, not only a performance delta
Mechanistic explanation of why, not just that, it works

selected.name: Operational Specificity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract specifies the essential mechanism, assumptions, data conditions, and evaluation setup well enough to reconstruct the contribution; score 0 when it consists mainly of slogans or unnamed architectural additions.
selected.rationale: R58 provides almost no operational content, while R32 and R54 describe broad architectural additions with limited detail about their concrete mechanisms.
member_names: Specificity of named failure modes in prior work

selected.name: Structural Inductive-Bias Fit
selected.instruction: Score 10 when domain structure, symmetry, constraints, or relational geometry is mapped to a specific architectural or objective choice and the preserved information is explained; score 0 when a fashionable mechanism is used without structural justification.
selected.rationale: R18 uses rotational symmetry, R43 uses spectral graph structure, and R52 uses higher-order relational structure to motivate their designs.

selected.name: Ambiguity Awareness
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the work recognizes multiple valid explanations, solutions, or latent rewards and designs its objective or inference procedure accordingly; score 0 when it assumes an unjustified unique target.
selected.rationale: R41 explicitly handles multiple valid combinatorial solutions, R04 addresses validity among many discrete sequences, and R50 confronts underdetermined rewards from demonstrations.

selected.name: Judgability from printed text alone, no title recognition
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the item text itself (title + abstract body) contains enough substantive description of motivation, method, and results to be judged on its own, without needing to recognize the paper from its title. A 10 = the abstract body fully describes what was done and found in prose. A 0 = the abstract body is missing or is a content-free stub (title only, or a placeholder), such that any score would have to rely on recognizing the paper rather than reading its content.
selected.rationale: R20 ('Quasi-Recurrent Neural Networks') has literally no abstract body -- only a title -- yet still receives card_pct=0.902, a very high scorecard percentile, which is only explicable if the judge scored based on recognizing this as a well-known paper rather than from the (absent) text, a direct violation of text-only scoring. Contrast with R42 (card_pct=0.145), which is also short but contains real content (a stated problem, method, and general result) and receives a much lower, more text-grounded card score -- showing the gradient this criterion should track.
member_names: Judgability from printed text alone, no title recognition
Substantive, checkable content actually present in the text

selected.name: Scarcity Leverage
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly exploits sparse data, limited interaction, scarce viewpoints, or tight computation through a reusable structural advantage; score 0 when it assumes abundant resources or merely reports generic efficiency.
selected.rationale: R01 leverages extremely limited gameplay, R42 transfers multi-view priors from scarce viewpoints, and R17 addresses ultra-high-resolution inputs under constrained computation.

selected.name: Assumption discipline
selected.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract states assumptions and boundary conditions precisely and distinguishes what holds in each regime; give 0 when claims sound universal while conditions remain unstated.
selected.rationale: R32 separates one-dimensional, general strongly convex, and quadratic cases; R40 distinguishes linear from nonlinear VAEs; R49 explicitly handles distribution mismatch through a synthetic HMM setting.

selected.name: New reusable dataset or benchmark contributed alongside method
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explicitly states that the paper contributes a NEW reusable dataset, benchmark, or testbed to the community (not just a method evaluated on existing data). A 10 = the abstract explicitly states a new dataset/benchmark is created and released. A 0 = the paper evaluates purely on existing benchmarks/datasets with no new data/resource contribution mentioned.
selected.rationale: R09 (dense_pct=0.618) states 'We will publicly release both datasets' as an explicit resource contribution, and R37 (dense_pct=0.731) generates and releases a new synthetic dataset (GINC) specifically to enable clean study of the phenomenon. Both are dense-favored. By contrast R47 (card_pct=0.966) evaluates on 86 pre-existing datasets with no new resource contributed, and R55 (card_pct=1.000) likewise contributes no new dataset -- both scorecard-favored despite offering nothing new to the community's data pool.
member_names: New reusable dataset or benchmark contributed alongside method

selected.name: Economy of mechanism relative to size of the consequence
selected.instruction: Score the ratio between how little the method asks and how much it claims. A 10: a mechanism statable in one clause (prune activations at random and rescale; freeze the classifier up to a scale; use a single modified diffusion kernel) paired with a consequence that is large, qualitative, or surprising. A 5: moderate machinery, moderate payoff. A 0: an elaborate apparatus - several new losses, encodings, hypernetworks, schedules, regularizers - whose stated payoff is a benchmark improvement of ordinary size. Penalize expensive-for-what-it-buys; reward cheap-for-what-it-buys. This is about the ratio, not about simplicity or ambition alone.
selected.rationale: R25, R36, R38 and R35 are all one-clause mechanisms carrying outsized claims and all sit dense-high with card .103-.457. The card-high side concentrates the opposite ratio: R28 spends its abstract on three named components plus a multi-task training procedure, R44 stacks a content-preservation loss, a CLS matching loss, a CLIP loss, a semantic divergence loss and a resampling strategy, R43 defines three amalgamation mechanisms plus perturbations. A bank of criteria scored independently and summed rewards each additional described component, so it systematically prices apparatus as evidence of substance.
member_names: Economy of mechanism relative to size of the consequence

selected.name: Theory-Practice Coupling
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the analysis directly constrains, explains, or predicts the behavior of the proposed method; score 0 when theory is detached from the method or offers only generic guarantees.
selected.rationale: R21 and R44 tie convergence or stability claims directly to their architectures, while R45 connects finite-width analysis to observable interpolation behavior.

selected.name: Long-range information preservation
selected.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract gives an explicit route for accessing information across many layers, hops, scales, or time steps and explains why it remains stable; give 0 when dependencies are only asserted or handled by adding depth.
selected.rationale: R05 constructs multi-scale graph information, R19 proves preservation of long-range graph information, and R55 adds graph reasoning for long-distance textual relationships.

selected.name: Headline rests on an idea rather than on a leaderboard position
selected.instruction: Score what the abstract's central claim would reduce to if the numbers were removed. A 10: a statable proposition survives - something is true, something is unnecessary, something works for this reason. A 5: an idea and a ranking claim share the load. A 0: nothing survives - the claim is exhausted by breadth and rank ('a large-scale protocol comprising N baselines, M search spaces and K datasets; we achieve new state-of-the-art'), so that the paper's identity is its position on a table. Breadth of evaluation is not penalized in itself; it is penalized when it is the whole of the claim.
selected.rationale: R50 is the pure case - a protocol of 12 baselines, 16 search spaces and 86 datasets, ending in a rank claim - and sits card .966 against dense .385; R56 (card 1.000 / dense .094), R48 (.919 / .568) and R21 (.927 / .449) are the same shape. R24, R25 and R58 lose nothing if their numbers are struck out, and sit card .030, .162 and .218. An itemized bank scores evaluation breadth, baseline count and result strength as separate positive items, so a paper whose only claim is a leaderboard position accumulates points on several items at once.
member_names: Headline rests on an idea rather than on a leaderboard position

selected.name: Claim-aligned validation
selected.instruction: Give 10 when the validation setup directly varies the phenomenon the paper addresses and includes a relevant control or comparison; give 0 when evaluation is only generic benchmarking unrelated to the proposed mechanism.
selected.rationale: R24 varies quantization bit-width, R43 tests progressive-reward and ordinary-reward settings, and R54 evaluates exact bounded perturbation robustness. Each evaluation mirrors the paper’s central technical claim.

selected.name: Contribution attribution
selected.instruction: Give 10 when the abstract describes ablations or controlled contrasts that isolate individual components, losses, or design choices; give 0 when no component-level contrast is described and attribution is impossible from the text.
selected.rationale: R58 identifies the likelihood loss as the culprit before introducing β-NLL, while R38 traces predictions to experimental artifacts and tests their removal. Both support component-level causal attribution.

selected.name: Grandiose opening framing vs narrow delivered contribution
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on the GAP between how sweeping/important the abstract's opening sentence claims the problem area to be, and how narrow/specific the actual technical contribution delivered later in the abstract turns out to be. A 10 = a sweeping opening claim ('one of the primary open questions in AI', 'bridging two fields') followed by a narrow, specific technical fix. A 0 = the opening framing is modest and proportionate to the actual scope of the contribution delivered.
selected.rationale: R47 (card_pct=0.966) opens by declaring HPO 'one of the primary open questions in AI' before delivering a specific rank-based surrogate model; R16 (card_pct=0.761) opens by claiming to 'bridge the two fields of finite-agent and infinite-agent games' before delivering a policy-conditioning hypernetwork. Both large opening claims relative to narrow deliveries are scorecard-favored (dense_pct 0.385 and 0.291 respectively), while R40 (dense_pct=0.996) opens with no grandiose framing at all, matching its narrow, direct technical scope.
member_names: Grandiose opening framing vs narrow delivered contribution

selected.name: Formalism density
selected.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract contains theorem, proof, bound, assumption, equation, or mathematically formal terminology; judge formalism extent only, not rigor, correctness, or research value.
selected.rationale: Theoretical training and community norms leave visible formal-language fingerprints, and may also affect genuine quality. R08 and R24 foreground bounds, phases, and influence-function analysis, while R44 emphasizes formal coreset guarantees.
member_names: Density of explicit numeric performance figures

selected.name: Evaluation breadth
selected.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract claims coverage across multiple datasets, languages, domains, tasks, architectures, or transfer settings; judge breadth of described coverage only, not whether it is adequate or convincing.
selected.rationale: Large teams and greater infrastructure can support broad evaluations, while also potentially improving genuine research quality. R04 spans up to 44 languages, and R11 reports 86 datasets across 16 search spaces.

selected.name: Enumerated contribution scaffolding and numbered-pitfall templates
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much explicit enumeration scaffolding the text uses: phrases like 'our contributions are three-fold', 'two common pitfalls: (1) ... (2) ...', 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ... Fourth, ...', 'We address this in two ways', numbered or lettered lists of problems or components. 0 = no enumeration language at all; 3 = a single ordinal marker used in passing; 6 = one clearly enumerated two-item list; 8 = an explicit contribution count plus an enumerated walkthrough; 10 = the whole abstract is organised as a numbered walkthrough of three or more items with an announced count. Score the presence and prominence of the enumeration template only. You must NOT judge whether the abstract is well organised, whether the enumerated contributions are real, or whether this structure aids the reader.
selected.rationale: This is a learnable writing template that makes an abstract trivially parseable by criterion-by-criterion scoring: each numbered item hands the judge a discrete thing to credit. Every clear instance in the slice sits on the same side of the disagreement: R40 ('Our contributions are three-fold. First ... Next ... Finally'), R17 ('First, ... Second, ... Third, ... Fourth, ...'), R02 ('two common pitfalls: (1) scalability ... (2) interpretability'), R48 ('Our contribution is two-fold. First ... Second ...') and R44 ('First ... Then ... Finally') are all dense_low_card_high, with card_pct from 0.517 to 0.893. Adopting a template is a stylistic habit, not evidence about the research.
member_names: Enumerated contribution scaffolding and numbered-pitfall templates

selected.name: Abstract length
selected.instruction: Rate from 0 (very brief) to 10 (very long) how much text, sentence count, and elaboration the abstract contains; judge extent only, not whether the additional detail is good or useful.
selected.rationale: Length is a visible verbosity proxy that can influence processing independently of research quality. R08 and R44 are highly elaborated, whereas R32 is only a title.

selected.name: Editorial polish
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of fluent grammar, consistent terminology, smooth transitions, and carefully standardized prose; judge only textual polish, not research quality.
selected.rationale: R47 and R54 use highly smooth, carefully staged exposition, while R31 and R49 contain visible grammatical awkwardness and less standardized phrasing. Professional editing can affect reception without itself being research quality.

selected.name: Acronym and method-name density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract introduces named methods, abbreviations, and component labels; judge only extent, not whether the naming is useful or technically good.
selected.rationale: R12 introduces PAPO and several named components, and R24 introduces HYSP alongside multiple specialized terms; R02 and R07 likewise foreground distinctive named methods.

selected.name: Trend/hype-keyword density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how many currently-fashionable subfield buzzwords appear in the abstract (e.g., 'GPT', 'in-context learning', 'diffusion', 'Transformer', 'large language model', 'foundation model'). 0 = no such terms appear; 10 = the abstract is dense with such terms throughout. Do not judge whether the use of these terms is warranted, accurate, or central to the contribution -- score only the raw presence of this vocabulary.
selected.rationale: R27 foregrounds 'GPT-3', 'in-context learning', and 'large language models' repeatedly, and R51 foregrounds 'diffusion-based' throughout; papers submitted while a topic is peaking may draw disproportionate attention from both a dense reader's learned priors and a scorecard's topic-relevance criteria, independent of the paper's own contribution quality (mixed since genuinely important work also clusters on hot topics).

selected.name: Code/data release statement presence
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how explicitly the abstract states that code, data, or trained models will be or are being released (e.g., a repository URL, 'code is available at...', 'we release our implementation'). 0 = no release statement of any kind; 10 = an explicit, specific release statement naming a repository. Do not judge whether releasing code says anything about the work's quality -- score only whether the statement is textually present.
selected.rationale: R07 and R28 both end with an explicit GitHub link and release statement while similarly-scoped papers like R08 and R11 make no release claim at all; packaging and hosting a public repo takes engineering time that better-resourced groups have more of, so this can be predictive of scorecard favor without being a research-quality signal per se (though well-resourced groups may also do better work, hence mixed).

selected.name: Formal-theory signaling
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses theorem, proof, bound, convergence, asymptotic, or formal mathematical-guarantee language; judge only extent, not correctness or importance.
selected.rationale: R04, R08, R29, R40, and R55 prominently use formal guarantees and asymptotic claims. Authorial training or seniority may produce this fingerprint and may also correlate with genuine technical quality, so it is mixed.

selected.name: Artifact-availability cues
selected.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract advertises code, pretrained models, datasets, repositories, or reproducibility artifacts; judge the presence of availability statements only, not whether the artifacts are useful or the research is sound.
selected.rationale: Well-supported groups and open-source-oriented communities leave artifact-sharing fingerprints, while those resources can also facilitate genuine quality. R07, R10, and R19 explicitly mention publicly available code or models.
